Press **Validate answers** to inspect each interpreted response, then **Check answer** to grade it. After an edit, validate again.

## For teachers

Choose a question to try, then change the response to see which mathematical distinctions its grading preserves. The [authoring guide](docs/authoring.qmd) explains how to bring your own questions to a page.

### Algebraic equivalence and written form

#### Equivalent rational expression

The prompt states the domain $x\ne -n$. A cancelled fraction and the original unreduced expression both receive full credit because the question asks for *any equivalent expression* on that domain. A reciprocal triggers a targeted feedback branch.

```{.stack-question}
#| file: questions/rational-equivalence.xml
#| question: Equivalent rational expression
#| variants: 3
#| seed: 29
#| review: true
#| feedback: true
#| label: rational-practice
#| feedback-policy: two-step-practice
```

[Download the rational question](questions/rational-equivalence.xml)

Its **AI Feedback** first asks a guiding question and then offers a worked explanation. The [teaching-policy setup](docs/authoring.qmd#choose-a-teaching-policy) shows how to choose a sequence for your own course.

### Numerical answers and precision

#### Three numerical checks

These fields demonstrate absolute tolerance, relative tolerance, and decimal-place precision. The final field distinguishes `17.5` from `17.50`, because the written precision is part of the task. Their response trees contribute 30%, 40%, and 30% of the total.

::: {#measurement-context .ai-context}
For a measured quantity, absolute tolerance compares $|x-a|$ to a fixed bound. Relative tolerance compares it to a fraction of the reference value. Written decimal places express the precision of a reported measurement.
:::

```{.stack-question}
#| file: questions/numerical-measurement.xml
#| question: Rectangle and triangle measurements
#| seed: 47
#| review: true
#| feedback: true
#| context: measurement-context
```

[Download the numerical question](questions/numerical-measurement.xml)

### Equations and logic

#### Zero product equations

Rewrite $ab=0$ as alternatives joined by `or`. Here `AlgEquiv` checks the
solutions represented by polynomial equations, including repeated-root
information; it is not simply comparing the strings on either side.

```{.stack-question}
#| file: questions/zero-product.xml
#| question: Zero product equations
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

[Download XML](questions/zero-product.xml)

#### Boolean equivalence

Use De Morgan's law to rewrite `not(a and b)` using `or`. In this question
`a` and `b` are propositions, and the checker compares their truth values
for every assignment in its supported finite domain.

```{.stack-question}
#| file: questions/boolean-equivalence.xml
#| question: Boolean equivalence
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

[Download XML](questions/boolean-equivalence.xml)

### Collections

#### Finite lists and sets {#finite-lists-and-sets}

Compare an ordered list with an unordered set. Lists retain positions and
repetitions; sets ignore order and repeated mathematical members. One field
also shows feedback about extra, missing or repeated set entries.

```{#finite-collections .stack-question}
#| file: questions/finite-collections.xml
#| question: Finite scalar collections
#| variants: 2
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

#### Nested collections and written form

Try a list containing another list and a set. The task keeps nested boundaries
and list order; a separate written-form check can distinguish repeated entries
or different arithmetic forms even when values agree.

```{#nested-collections .stack-question}
#| file: questions/nested-collections.xml
#| question: Nested finite collections
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

### Matrix conditions

#### Find a nonidentity matrix with determinant one

Enter **any integer $2\times2$ matrix with determinant 1, except the identity**.
Each of the three conditions earns one third of the score: integer entries,
determinant one, and nonidentity. You are finding a matrix that satisfies
conditions, rather than copying a displayed model answer.

```{#determinant-one .stack-question}
#| file: questions/determinant-one.xml
#| question: A nonidentity integer matrix with determinant one
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
#| feedback: true
#| context: none
```

[Download XML](questions/determinant-one.xml)

The question uses three normal response trees, one per condition. The
Python-only `MatrixProperty` checks each condition; see [which matrix test to
choose](docs/python-checker-api.qmd#choose-the-mathematical-test).

#### Symmetric positive definite matrix {#symmetric-positive-definite-matrix}

Give any $2\times2$ matrix with **both** symmetry and positive definiteness,
using integers or exact fractions. Symmetry means $A=A^T$; positive
definiteness means $x^T A x>0$ for every nonzero real $x$. The identity and
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ both pass. The combined `is_spd`
checker makes one decision and its response tree awards full credit only for
both conditions. Compare this with the separate-check question below, and
see [all four mathematical outcomes](docs/python-checker-api.qmd#symmetric-positive-definite-matrices).

```{.stack-question #spd-example}
#| file: questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml
#| question: A symmetric positive definite matrix
#| python-checkers: questions/spd-checker.py
#| review: true
```

[Download question XML](questions/symmetric-positive-definite.xml) ·
[View the complete Python checker](questions/spd-checker.py)

#### Symmetry and positive definiteness separately {#symmetry-and-positive-definiteness-separately}

This version has two response trees. One checks symmetry; the other checks
positive definiteness through $x^T A x>0$. Each condition earns half the
marks. Try $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$: it is positive definite
but not symmetric, so it earns the positivity half. Try
$\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ for symmetry without positive
definiteness. For the exact criterion and a four-case comparison, see the
[teacher explanation](docs/python-checker-api.qmd#symmetric-positive-definite-matrices).

```{.stack-question #spd-separate-example}
#| file: questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml
#| question: Symmetry and positive definiteness separately
#| python-checkers: questions/spd-checker.py
#| review: true
```

[Download the two-PRT XML](questions/symmetric-positive-definite-prt.xml) ·
[See how to author either scoring policy](docs/python-checker-api.qmd#author-the-spd-checker)

### Rank and bases {#matrix-problems-from-ingmat-3a}

These three questions adapt a linear algebra course's rank and null-space exercises.

#### Rank and pivot columns: ordinary STACK answer tests

This question uses `AlgEquiv` and two equally weighted response trees. The rank
and the complete ordered pivot list each earn half the total.

```{#course-b-rank-pivots .stack-question}
#| file: questions/course-b-rank-pivots.xml
#| question: Rank and pivot columns of B
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

[Download XML](questions/course-b-rank-pivots.xml)

#### A basis for the null space of B

Put one proposed basis vector in each column. A basis is not a unique matrix:
changing a vector’s nonzero scale can still give a correct answer. Choose the
number of columns before validating. `IsBasis` checks the space defined by
the original matrix $B$, not just the entries of one model basis.

```{#course-b-nullspace .stack-question}
#| file: questions/course-b-nullspace.xml
#| question: A basis for the null space of B
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

[Download XML](questions/course-b-nullspace.xml)

#### A basis for the null space of C

Here you may reorder or combine basis vectors, provided your columns remain
independent and span the null space of $C$. Entry-by-entry equality with one
model matrix would reject many correct answers. `IsBasis` uses the original
matrix $C$ to define the target space.

```{#course-c-nullspace .stack-question}
#| file: questions/course-c-nullspace.xml
#| question: A basis for the null space of C
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

[Download XML](questions/course-c-nullspace.xml)

For both basis questions, **green** marks a nonzero vector in the target space
when the valid submitted vectors are independent. A green family can still be
incomplete. **Yellow** marks every member of a dependent valid family;
**red** marks a zero vector or one outside the space. The whole answer earns
credit only when it is a complete basis. Colors explain the result but do not
award partial marks. Editing or resizing clears them.

Read [how to author a basis question](docs/python-checker-api.qmd#basis-questions-use-the-matrix-in-the-question)
or [configure its matrix input](docs/matrix-input.qmd).


### A custom scalar rule

#### Custom Python checker {#custom-python-checker}

Enter any positive integer multiple of the displayed number. A named
`PythonChecker` function decides whether the submitted integer has the
required property; the question's ordinary response tree awards credit.
See the [author API](docs/python-checker-api.qmd#pythonchecker-api-and-a-scalar-example).

```{.stack-question #python-multiple}
#| file: questions/python-checker.xml
#| question: A positive integer multiple (PythonChecker)
#| python-checkers: questions/checkers.py
#| variants: 3
#| seed: 17
#| review: true
```

## For developers

Use the [authoring guide](docs/authoring.qmd) for imports, question options,
tests and AI Feedback policies. The [Python answer-test guide](docs/python-checker-api.qmd)
explains the basis and property choices and gives the complete SPD checker
walkthrough. The questions above link to their XML; the SPD example also links
to its Python file. The rational activity chooses the `two-step-practice`
policy, while other feedback activities inherit a four-step sequence; see
[policy setup](docs/authoring.qmd#choose-a-teaching-policy). Run authored tests
and inspect alternate correct answers before publishing.

## Sources

The determinant-one question adapts a [math-exercise custom-assessment example](https://erasmus-ctm.github.io/math-exercise/custom-assessment.html);
its [provenance record](questions/determinant-example-provenance.json) gives
the adaptation and license. The rank/pivot and null-space questions adapt
[INGMat 3A week 3 exercises](https://aacchhee.github.io/ingmat3a_ntnu/pages/uke3.html#uke3-stotte-oppgaver)
under CC BY-SA 4.0; their [source record](questions/course-examples-provenance.json)
identifies the exact originals. The unchanged imported questions come from
the STACK collection, with [individual source and license details](questions/upstream/sources.json).
